claim: Puromycin is an amino-acyl transfer RNA analog widely employed in studies of protein synthesis.
source: Puromycin is an amino-acyl transfer RNA analog widely employed in studies of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about puromycin's structure and use.

claim: Puromycin is covalently incorporated into nascent polypeptide chains.
source: Since puromycin is covalently incorporated into nascent polypeptide chains, anti-puromycin immunofluorescence enables visualization of nascent protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about puromycin's mechanism of action.

claim: Anti-puromycin immunofluorescence enables visualization of nascent protein synthesis.
source: Since puromycin is covalently incorporated into nascent polypeptide chains, anti-puromycin immunofluorescence enables visualization of nascent protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the use of anti-puromycin antibodies.

claim: A common assumption in studies of local messenger RNA translation is that anti-puromycin staining of puromycylated nascent polypeptides in fixed cells accurately reports on their original site of translation, particularly when ribosomes are stalled with elongation inhibitors prior to puromycin treatment.
source: A common assumption in studies of local messenger RNA translation is that the anti-puromycin staining of puromycylated nascent polypeptides in fixed cells accurately reports on their original site of translation, particularly when ribosomes are stalled with elongation inhibitors prior to puromycin treatment.
evidence: This describes a common assumption in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: When attempting to implement a proximity ligation assay to detect ribosome-puromycin complexes, no evidence was found to support the assumption that puromycylated nascent polypeptides remain at their original site of translation.
source: However, when we attempted to implement a proximity ligation assay to detect ribosome-puromycin complexes, we found no evidence to support this assumption.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Puromycylated nascent polypeptides rapidly dissociate from ribosomes even in the presence of elongation inhibitors.
source: We further demonstrated, using biochemical assays and live cell imaging of nascent polypeptides in mammalian cells, that puromycylated nascent polypeptides rapidly dissociate from ribosomes even in the presence of elongation inhibitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental work using biochemical assays and live cell imaging.

claim: Attempts to define precise subcellular translation sites using anti-puromycin immunostaining may be confounded by release of puromycylated nascent polypeptide chains prior to fixation.
source: Our results suggest that attempts to define precise subcellular translation sites using anti-puromycin immunostaining may be confounded by release of puromycylated nascent polypeptide chains prior to fixation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing rapid dissociation of puromycylated nascent chains.

claim: Subcellular localization of messenger RNA (mRNA) translation enables dynamic, rapid regulation of protein synthesis in a wide range of biological systems.
source: Subcellular localization of messenger RNA (mRNA) translation enables dynamic, rapid regulation of protein synthesis in a wide range of biological systems (Buxbaum et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2014; Martin and Ephrussi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The number of localized mRNAs is much greater than originally appreciated.
source: The number of localized mRNAs is much greater than originally appreciated (Lécuyer et al., 2007), and the study of subcellular translation sites is now an area of active research across multiple organisms and cell types.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Puromycin enters the ribosomal aminoacyl-tRNA binding site (A site) and is covalently coupled to the carboxyl-activated NPC at the ribosomal peptidyl-tRNA binding site (P site).
source: As an amino-acyl transfer RNA (tRNA) analog, puromycin enters the ribosomal aminoacyl-tRNA binding site (A site) and is covalently coupled to the carboxyl-activated NPC at the ribosomal peptidyl-tRNA binding site (P site) that is adjacent to the A site within the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center (PTC), terminating protein synthesis and ejecting a C-terminal puromycylated NPC (Nathans, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature describing the mechanism of puromycin action.

claim: Puromycin terminates protein synthesis and ejects a C-terminal puromycylated NPC.
source: As an amino-acyl transfer RNA (tRNA) analog, puromycin enters the ribosomal aminoacyl-tRNA binding site (A site) and is covalently coupled to the carboxyl-activated NPC at the ribosomal peptidyl-tRNA binding site (P site) that is adjacent to the A site within the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center (PTC), terminating protein synthesis and ejecting a C-terminal puromycylated NPC (Nathans, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature describing the mechanism of puromycin action.

claim: Fluorescent puromycin analogues were first used to label nascent polypeptides.
source: This reaction was first exploited to label nascent polypeptides with fluorescent puromycin analogues (Nemoto et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2005; Starck et al., 2004), and became widely used both in vitro and in vivo following the development of anti-puromycin antibodies (Schmidt et al., 2009) and 'click'-chemistry-compatible puromycin analogues (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Puromycin labeling became widely used following the development of anti-puromycin antibodies and 'click'-chemistry-compatible puromycin analogues.
source: This reaction was first exploited to label nascent polypeptides with fluorescent puromycin analogues (Nemoto et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2005; Starck et al., 2004), and became widely used both in vitro and in vivo following the development of anti-puromycin antibodies (Schmidt et al., 2009) and 'click'-chemistry-compatible puromycin analogues (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Using puromycin labeling to visualize the subcellular distribution of nascent protein synthesis in specific cell types within complex tissues remains challenging.
source: Despite technical advances, using puromycin labeling to visualize the subcellular distribution of nascent protein synthesis in specific cell types within complex tissues remains challenging.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges in the field.

claim: Levels of protein synthesis in dendrites and axons are relatively low compared to neighboring neuronal and glial cell bodies in polarized cells such as neurons.
source: This is particularly true for polarized cells such as neurons, where levels of protein synthesis in dendrites and axons are relatively low compared to neighboring neuronal and glial cell bodies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein synthesis in neurons.

claim: Large nerve terminals may be readily visualized using puromycin labeling.
source: Although large nerve terminals may be readily visualized (Scarnati et al., 2018) and expansion microscopy can provide higher resolution (Hafner et al., 2019), diffusion or trafficking of puromycylated NPCs prior to chemical fixation may confound attempts to determine the original translation site.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expansion microscopy can provide higher resolution for visualizing puromycin labeling.
source: Although large nerve terminals may be readily visualized (Scarnati et al., 2018) and expansion microscopy can provide higher resolution (Hafner et al., 2019), diffusion or trafficking of puromycylated NPCs prior to chemical fixation may confound attempts to determine the original translation site.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Diffusion or trafficking of puromycylated NPCs prior to chemical fixation may confound attempts to determine the original translation site.
source: Although large nerve terminals may be readily visualized (Scarnati et al., 2018) and expansion microscopy can provide higher resolution (Hafner et al., 2019), diffusion or trafficking of puromycylated NPCs prior to chemical fixation may confound attempts to determine the original translation site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of puromycylated NPCs.

claim: David et al., 2012 introduced the ribopuromycylation (RPM) assay and used it to argue in favor of active protein synthesis within the nucleus.
source: To combat this problem, David et al., 2012 introduced the ribopuromycylation (RPM) assay and used it to argue in favor of active protein synthesis within the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The premise of the RPM assay is that pretreatment of cells with elongation inhibitors, such as emetine or cycloheximide, prevents release of puromycylated nascent chains from translating ribosomes.
source: The premise of the RPM assay is that pretreatment of cells with elongation inhibitors, such as emetine or cycloheximide, prevents release of puromycylated nascent chains from translating ribosomes (Bastide et al., 2018; David et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing the RPM assay.

claim: The RPM assay asserts that anti-puromycin immunostaining of labeled nascent chains in fixed cells occurs in situ on elongation-stalled ribosomes bound to mRNA.
source: These studies assert that anti-puromycin immunostaining of labeled nascent chains in fixed cells occurs in situ on elongation-stalled ribosomes bound to mRNA.
evidence: This is a description of the claims made by previous studies.

claim: Elongation inhibitors do not prevent the release of puromycylated NPCs from ribosomes.
source: In the course of our studies, we found that elongation inhibitors do not prevent the release of puromycylated NPCs from ribosomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Structural modeling revealed that antibodies are unlikely to be able to directly contact and recognize puromycin within the PTC of intact ribosomes due to steric hindrance.
source: Furthermore, structural modeling revealed that antibodies are unlikely to be able to directly contact and recognize puromycin within the PTC of intact ribosomes due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is a finding from structural modeling analysis.

claim: Anti-puromycin immunostaining occurs only on puromycylated nascent chains released from ribosomes.
source: Together, these results suggest that anti-puromycin immunostaining occurs only on puromycylated nascent chains released from ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and structural modeling.

claim: The eL22-HA/Puro PLA produced a robust fluorescent signal in RiboTag glioma cells treated with puromycin.
source: Similar to anti-puromycin IF, the eL22-HA/Puro PLA produced a robust fluorescent signal in RiboTag glioma cells treated with puromycin, which was blocked by pretreatment with anisomycin, an antibiotic that binds to the A-site 'cleft' and competitively inhibits puromycin incorporation (Hansen et al., 2003; Pestka et al., 1972).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Anisomycin pretreatment blocked the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal.
source: Similar to anti-puromycin IF, the eL22-HA/Puro PLA produced a robust fluorescent signal in RiboTag glioma cells treated with puromycin, which was blocked by pretreatment with anisomycin, an antibiotic that binds to the A-site 'cleft' and competitively inhibits puromycin incorporation (Hansen et al., 2003; Pestka et al., 1972).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Anisomycin binds to the A-site 'cleft' and competitively inhibits puromycin incorporation.
source: Similar to anti-puromycin IF, the eL22-HA/Puro PLA produced a robust fluorescent signal in RiboTag glioma cells treated with puromycin, which was blocked by pretreatment with anisomycin, an antibiotic that binds to the A-site 'cleft' and competitively inhibits puromycin incorporation (Hansen et al., 2003; Pestka et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal was specific to the presence of both antibodies.
source: We verified that the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal was specific to the presence of both antibodies by omitting either the anti-puromycin or the anti-HA antibody (Figure 1C, see Figure 1—source data 1 for statistics)
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1C.

claim: U87 glioma cells do not express eL22-HA.
source: We further tested the cell-type specificity of the eL22-HA/Puro PLA using human U87 glioma cells, which do not express eL22-HA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: U87 glioma cells exhibit minimal eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal despite robust anti-puro IF labeling.
source: As expected, these cells exhibit minimal eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal despite robust anti-puro IF labeling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Quantification of eL22-HA/Puro PLA puncta per cell revealed ~200 puncta per cell.
source: Quantification of eL22-HA/Puro PLA puncta per cell revealed ~200 puncta per cell, while omission of either puromycin or HA antibodies reduced this to <8 puncta per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Omission of either puromycin or HA antibodies reduced eL22-HA/Puro PLA puncta to <8 puncta per cell.
source: Quantification of eL22-HA/Puro PLA puncta per cell revealed ~200 puncta per cell, while omission of either puromycin or HA antibodies reduced this to <8 puncta per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the absence of elongation inhibitors, puromycylated NPCs dissociate from ribosomes in minutes.
source: Previous imaging studies have demonstrated that in the absence of elongation inhibitors, puromycylated NPCs dissociate from ribosomes in minutes (Morisaki et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016, see also below).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Emetine pretreatment produced a minor, but statistically significant, decrease in the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal relative to the corresponding anti-puromycin IF.
source: However, emetine pretreatment produced a minor, but statistically significant, decrease in the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal relative to the corresponding anti-puromycin IF (Figure 1C) and relative to eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal from cells receiving no pretreatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Emetine pretreatment produced a minor, but statistically significant, decrease in the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal relative to eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal from cells receiving no pretreatment.
source: However, emetine pretreatment produced a minor, but statistically significant, decrease in the eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal relative to the corresponding anti-puromycin IF (Figure 1C) and relative to eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal from cells receiving no pretreatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effect of emetine was specific to eL22-HA/Puro PLA, as emetine pretreatment did not significantly alter anti-puromycin IF.
source: This effect of emetine was specific to eL22-HA/Puro PLA, as emetine pretreatment did not significantly alter anti-puromycin IF (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After up to 45 min of puromycin washout, the eL22-HA/Puro PLA still produced intense signal comparable to anti-puromycin IF.
source: After up to 45 min of washout, the eL22-HA/Puro PLA still produced intense signal comparable to anti-puromycin IF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Harringtonine stalls newly initiating ribosomes.
source: Since the small-molecule drug harringtonine stalls newly initiating ribosomes (Fresno et al., 1977), extended incubation in harringtonine eliminates the presence of NPCs once elongating ribosomes are runoff.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Extended incubation in harringtonine eliminates the presence of NPCs once elongating ribosomes are runoff.
source: Since the small-molecule drug harringtonine stalls newly initiating ribosomes (Fresno et al., 1977), extended incubation in harringtonine eliminates the presence of NPCs once elongating ribosomes are runoff.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of harringtonine action.

claim: Harringtonine runoff before puromycin treatment removed NPCs available for puromycylation.
source: We first confirmed that harringtonine runoff removed NPCs available for puromycylation by conducting the harringtonine runoff before puromycin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Conducting harringtonine runoff after puromycin treatment and washout still produced robust eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal that was only slightly reduced relative the corresponding anti-puromycin IF.
source: However, conducting harringtonine runoff after puromycin treatment and washout still produced robust eL22-HA/Puro PLA signal that was only slightly reduced relative the corresponding anti-puromycin IF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The eL22-HA/Puro PLA reports primarily on the cytoplasmic abundance of puromycylated NPCs, regardless of whether they are currently bound to ribosomes.
source: Therefore, we conclude that while the eL22-HA/Puro PLA is specific for the presence of antigen and antibody, it reports primarily on the cytoplasmic abundance of puromycylated NPCs, regardless of whether they are currently bound to ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PLA is generally assumed to produce signals based only on specific proximity (i.e. antigen-antigen interaction) given the distance requirement of <40 nm.
source: The results of our eL22-HA/Puro PLA were somewhat surprising, since PLA is generally assumed to produce signals based only on specific proximity (i.e. antigen-antigen interaction) given the distance requirement of <40 nm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PLA technique.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that PLA signals can be generated by a variety of non-interacting antigen pairs, provided they have overlapping spatial distributions and are present at high concentrations.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that PLA signals can be generated by a variety of non-interacting antigen pairs, provided they have overlapping spatial distributions and are present at high concentrations (Alsemarz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cycloheximide binds to the ribosomal large, 60S, subunit in the tRNA 'exit' site (E site), stalling elongation by preventing exit of the deacylated E-site tRNA.
source: Cycloheximide binds to the ribosomal large, 60S, subunit in the tRNA 'exit' site (E site), stalling elongation by preventing exit of the deacylated E-site tRNA (Schneider-Poetsch et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Emetine acts similarly to pactamycin, binding the ribosomal small, 40S, subunit in the E site and preventing translocation of the tRNA-mRNA complex.
source: Emetine acts similarly to pactamycin, binding the ribosomal small, 40S, subunit in the E site and preventing translocation of the tRNA-mRNA complex (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous imaging studies demonstrated that puromycylated NPCs are released from ribosomes in the presence of cycloheximide.
source: In fact, previous imaging studies demonstrated that puromycylated NPCs are released from ribosomes in the presence of cycloheximide (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Puromycin immunoreactivity was undetectable in polysome fractions from cells pretreated with emetine or cycloheximide prior to puromycin treatment.
source: We found that puromycin immunoreactivity was undetectable in polysome fractions, and that puromycylated NPCs were abundant primarily in the top two fractions corresponding to free material (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Puromycylated NPCs were abundant primarily in the top two fractions corresponding to free material in sucrose gradient fractionation.
source: We found that puromycin immunoreactivity was undetectable in polysome fractions, and that puromycylated NPCs were abundant primarily in the top two fractions corresponding to free material (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The absence of puromycylated NPCs in polysome fractions of cells treated with puromycin, even after pretreatment with elongation inhibitors, is consistent with previous work.
source: The absence of puromycylated NPCs in polysome fractions of cells treated with puromycin, even after pretreatment with elongation inhibitors, is consistent with previous work (Colombo et al., 1965; Grollman, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: David et al., 2012 bound untreated polysomes to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes before puromycin treatment, fixation, and immuno-ELISA.
source: However, these results seem to contradict those of David et al., 2012, who first bound untreated polysomes to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes before puromycin treatment, fixation, and immuno-ELISA.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in previous work.

claim: Puromycylated NPCs could directly bind to the PVDF matrix, creating the appearance that they are still tethered to ribosomes.
source: Since puromycylated NPCs are released from polysomes either prior to or during sucrose gradient centrifugation (Figure 2A–B), we suspected that puromycylated NPCs would also be released from polysomes bound to PVDF (David et al., 2012). However, puromycylated NPCs could directly bind to the PVDF matrix, creating the appearance that they are still tethered to ribosomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the discrepancy with previous work.

claim: Western blotting of captured proteins from immunoprecipitation experiments showed no evidence of co-IP: puromycin immunoreactivity was observed only in anti-puromycin IP samples, while eL22-HA and Rps6 immunoreactivity were observed only in anti-HA IP samples.
source: Regardless of emetine pretreatment, western blotting of captured proteins showed no evidence of co-IP: puromycin immunoreactivity was observed only in anti-puromycin IP samples, while eL22-HA and Rps6 immunoreactivity were observed only in anti-HA IP samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Emetine pretreatment did not prevent release of puromycylated NPCs from ribosomes.
source: Although emetine pretreatment did not prevent release of puromycylated NPCs from ribosomes (Figure 2A–D), the RNA captured by eL22-HA IP confirmed that emetine inhibits polysome breakdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: RNA captured by eL22-HA IP confirmed that emetine inhibits polysome breakdown.
source: Although emetine pretreatment did not prevent release of puromycylated NPCs from ribosomes (Figure 2A–D), the RNA captured by eL22-HA IP confirmed that emetine inhibits polysome breakdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNA captured by anti-HA IP from emetine pretreated cells had a significantly higher total yield and a lower ratio of 60S subunit 28S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) to 40S subunit 18S rRNA (28S/18S ratio), reflecting enhanced capture of intact polysomes in the presence of emetine.
source: RNA captured by anti-HA IP from emetine pretreated cells had a significantly higher total yield and a lower ratio of 60S subunit 28S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) to 40S subunit 18S rRNA (28S/18S ratio), reflecting enhanced capture of intact polysomes in the presence of emetine (and enhanced capture of HA-tagged free 60S subunits in the absence of emetine).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: No detectable rRNA was captured by anti-puromycin IP, even with emetine pretreatment.
source: In contrast to the anti-HA IP, no detectable rRNA was captured by anti-puromycin IP, even with emetine pretreatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Although emetine prevents polysome breakdown by puromycin, it does not prevent release of puromycylated NPCs.
source: These results are consistent with the work of Grollman, 1968 and suggest that although emetine prevents polysome breakdown by puromycin, it does not prevent release of puromycylated NPCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The SunTag translation reporter system comprises an mRNA encoding the SunTag array of 24 GCN4 repeats followed by oxBFP and an auxin-induced degron (AID), super folder green fluorescent protein (sfGFP)-bound single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of GCN4 antibody (scFv-GCN4-sfGFP), and Oryza Sativa transport inhibitor response 1 (OsTIR1) to remove completed proteins containing the AID.
source: We employed the version of this system described by Wu et al., 2016, which comprises (i) an mRNA encoding the SunTag array of 24 GCN4 repeats followed by oxBFP and an auxin-induced degron (AID), (ii) super folder green fluorescent protein (sfGFP)-bound single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of GCN4 antibody (scFv-GCN4-sfGFP), and (iii) Oryza Sativa transport inhibitor response 1 (OsTIR1) to remove completed proteins containing the AID (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system used, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The soluble scFV-GCN4-sfGFP binds rapidly to the SunTag array present in NPCs as they emerge from the ribosome.
source: Because the soluble scFV-GCN4-sfGFP binds rapidly to the SunTag array (Tanenbaum et al., 2014) present in NPCs as they emerge from the ribosome, polysomes translating the reporter are visualized as bright spots (hereafter SunTag puncta) on top of the cytoplasmic background fluorescence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Polysomes translating the SunTag reporter are visualized as bright spots (SunTag puncta) on top of the cytoplasmic background fluorescence.
source: Because the soluble scFV-GCN4-sfGFP binds rapidly to the SunTag array (Tanenbaum et al., 2014) present in NPCs as they emerge from the ribosome, polysomes translating the reporter are visualized as bright spots (hereafter SunTag puncta) on top of the cytoplasmic background fluorescence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SunTag puncta disappear in minutes upon treatment with puromycin.
source: Consistent with previous work (Morisaki et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016), we found that the SunTag puncta disappear in minutes upon treatment with puromycin (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3B, consistent with previous literature.

claim: The fading of SunTag puncta into the cytoplasmic background is caused by GFP-bound puromycylated NPCs diffusing away from polysome complexes.
source: Thus, the fading of SunTag puncta into the cytoplasmic background is caused by GFP-bound puromycylated NPCs diffusing away from polysome complexes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of the SunTag system and the observed data.

claim: Cycloheximide pretreatment slowed, but did not prevent, the disappearance of SunTag puncta.
source: Consistent with previous work (Wang et al., 2016), we found that cycloheximide pretreatment slowed, but did not prevent, the disappearance of SunTag puncta (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3C, consistent with previous literature.

claim: A previous report on cycloheximide-pretreated polysome lysates found that 50% of nascent peptides were released in a 30 s exposure to puromycin, while complete release was observed with a 5 min exposure.
source: A previous report on cycloheximide-pretreated polysome lysates found that 50% of nascent peptides were released in a 30 s exposure to puromycin, while complete release was observed with a 5 min exposure (Colombo et al., 1965).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A 30 s puromycin exposure caused complete release of nascent chains from untreated polysomes.
source: The same 30 s puromycin exposure caused complete release of nascent chains from untreated polysomes (Colombo et al., 1965), suggesting that cycloheximide slows the rate of puromycin binding to ribosomes and/or to nascent chains.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cycloheximide slows the rate of puromycin binding to ribosomes and/or to nascent chains.
source: The same 30 s puromycin exposure caused complete release of nascent chains from untreated polysomes (Colombo et al., 1965), suggesting that cycloheximide slows the rate of puromycin binding to ribosomes and/or to nascent chains.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous literature.

claim: Wang et al., 2016 proposed that the conformation of the ribosomal pre-translocation complex that is stabilized by cycloheximide causes crowding of the A site and slows the ability of puromycin to covalently react with the NPC.
source: These observations are consistent with our results (Figure 3C) and with recent work by Wang et al., 2016, who proposed that the conformation of the ribosomal pre-translocation complex that is stabilized by cycloheximide causes crowding of the A site and slows the ability of puromycin to covalently react with the NPC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No evidence was found that elongation is required for the release process of puromycylated NPCs.
source: Although we cannot exclude that cycloheximide also slows the release kinetics of NPCs once they have been transferred to puromycin, we found no evidence that elongation is required for the release process (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Emetine pretreatment enhanced the initial puromycin-induced release kinetics compared to puromycin alone.
source: In contrast to cycloheximide, emetine pretreatment enhanced the initial puromycin-induced release kinetics compared to puromycin alone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Emetine pretreatment eliminated the apparent lag phase seen in cells treated with puromycin or cycloheximide-puromycin.
source: Although emetine pretreatment eliminated the apparent lag phase seen in cells treated with puromycin or cycloheximide-puromycin, it slightly slowed the overall decay rate compared to puromycin alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Emetine pretreatment slightly slowed the overall decay rate of SunTag puncta compared to puromycin alone.
source: Although emetine pretreatment eliminated the apparent lag phase seen in cells treated with puromycin or cycloheximide-puromycin, it slightly slowed the overall decay rate compared to puromycin alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work.

claim: Emetine pretreated cells lost one-third of SunTag puncta significantly faster than those treated with puromycin alone.
source: Emetine pretreated cells lost one-third of SunTag puncta significantly faster than those treated with puromycin alone (Figure 3D, Welch's t-test for time at 66.6% remaining: t(5) = 3.932, p=0.0271), but the effect was smaller for half-life (Welch's t-test for time at 50% remaining: t(5) = 3.183, p=0.0294) and was no longer significant when two-thirds of puncta were lost (Welch's t-test for time at 33.3% remaining: t(5) = 0.967, p=0.3996).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: It is possible that emetine-bound ribosomes have either a higher affinity for puromycin and/or an enhanced reaction efficiency upon binding.
source: Although the mechanisms underlying these kinetic differences remain unknown, it is possible that emetine-bound ribosomes have either a higher affinity for puromycin and/or an enhanced reaction efficiency upon binding.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed kinetic differences.

claim: A model of emetine-bound ribosomes having higher affinity for puromycin and/or enhanced reaction efficiency is consistent with previous work describing enhanced puromycin incorporation in the presence of emetine.
source: Such a model is consistent with previous work describing enhanced puromycin incorporation in the presence of emetine (David et al., 2012), particularly at low temperatures (David et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Puromycylated NPCs are rapidly released from ribosomes even when cells are pretreated with emetine.
source: Regardless, these data clearly show that puromycylated NPCs are rapidly released from ribosomes even when cells are pretreated with emetine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: For puromycylated NPCs to truly remain 'tethered' to ribosomes, the puromycin would have to be localized in either the PTC or in the proximity of the nascent polypeptide exit tunnel.
source: For puromycylated NPCs to truly remain 'tethered' to ribosomes, the puromycin would have to be localized in either the PTC or in the proximity of the nascent polypeptide exit tunnel.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for puromycylated NPCs to remain tethered to ribosomes.

claim: It is conceivable that a few puromycin-terminated NPCs might become chemically fixed inside ribosomes despite the rapid kinetics of puromycylated NPC release.
source: Despite the rapid kinetics of puromycylated NPC release, it is conceivable that a few puromycin-terminated NPCs might become chemically fixed inside ribosomes.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible scenario.

claim: It is inconceivable that the antigen binding fragment (Fab) of an immunoglobulin G (IgG) molecule could access puromycin within the narrow, constricted geometry of the exit tunnel.
source: It is inconceivable that the antigen binding fragment (Fab) of an immunoglobulin G (IgG) molecule could access puromycin within the narrow, constricted geometry of the exit tunnel, so we focused our structural modeling on the PTC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure of the ribosome exit tunnel and the size of antibodies.

claim: A 2.8 Å cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a stalled mammalian 80S ribosomal complex containing a P-site tRNA was used for structural modeling.
source: We used a 2.8 Å cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a stalled mammalian 80S ribosomal complex containing a P-site tRNA (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019) and a 2.8 Å X-ray crystallographic structure of an intact mouse IgG2a monoclonal antibody (Harris et al., 1997), the exact isotype of the anti-puromycin clone 12D10 used in our study and in many others (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the structural data used for modeling, supported by citations.

claim: A 2.8 Å X-ray crystallographic structure of an intact mouse IgG2a monoclonal antibody was used for structural modeling.
source: We used a 2.8 Å cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a stalled mammalian 80S ribosomal complex containing a P-site tRNA (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019) and a 2.8 Å X-ray crystallographic structure of an intact mouse IgG2a monoclonal antibody (Harris et al., 1997), the exact isotype of the anti-puromycin clone 12D10 used in our study and in many others (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the structural data used for modeling, supported by citations.

claim: The IgG2a structure used is the exact isotype of the anti-puromycin clone 12D10 used in the study and in many others.
source: We used a 2.8 Å cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a stalled mammalian 80S ribosomal complex containing a P-site tRNA (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019) and a 2.8 Å X-ray crystallographic structure of an intact mouse IgG2a monoclonal antibody (Harris et al., 1997), the exact isotype of the anti-puromycin clone 12D10 used in our study and in many others (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the antibody used, supported by citations.

claim: Docking the IgG2a Fab within the A site such that the antigen binding site of the variable fragment was within ~6 Å or closer of puromycin immediately presented with obvious steric clashes between the Fab and multiple sites encompassing the 60S subunit ribosomal proteins, 28S rRNA, and P-site tRNA.
source: After we positioned puromycin within the PTC of the 80S ribosomal complex (see Materials and methods), we docked the IgG2a Fab within the A site such that the antigen binding site of the variable fragment was within ~6 Å or closer of puromycin. Such a model immediately presented with obvious steric clashes between the Fab and multiple sites encompassing the 60S subunit ribosomal proteins, 28S rRNA, and P-site tRNA (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The MolProbity Clashscores for twelve distinct Fab positions within the A site ranged from 85.79 to 246.3.
source: We analyzed the steric clashes resulting from twelve distinct Fab positions within the A site (see Materials and methods) using MolProbity to analyze ribosomal and tRNA residues located within a 12 Å radius of the Fab (Chen et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2018). The MolProbity Clashscores, the number of serious steric overlaps (>0.4 Å) per 1000 atoms, ranged from 85.79 to 246.3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All MolProbity Clashscores for the Fab docked in the A site were in the 0th percentile of all structures solved by cryo-EM to any resolution in the Protein Data Bank.
source: All of these MolProbity Clashscores were in the 0th percentile of all structures solved by cryo-EM to any resolution in the Protein Data Bank, that is there were no cryo-EM structures solved to any resolution with worse Clashscores (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The individual structures of the 80S ribosomal complex and IgG2a each have MolProbity Clashscores < 21.
source: In contrast, the individual structures of the 80S ribosomal complex and IgG2a each have MolProbity Clashscores < 21 (Figure 4B) and are in the 87th percentile of all cryo-EM structures solved to any resolution or of all X-ray crystallographic structures solved to similar resolutions, respectively (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The 'best' fit scenario for positioning the Fab as close as possible to puromycin within the A site while minimizing steric clashes generated a MolProbity score of 22.89, representing the 25th percentile of all cryo-EM structures solved to any resolution.
source: Next, we attempted to model the Fab fragment so it was positioned as close as possible to puromycin within the A site of the 80S ribosomal complex but in such a manner so as to minimize steric clashes. This model generated a MolProbity score of 22.89, representing the 25th percentile of all cryo-EM structures solved to any resolution (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: For the 'best' fit scenario, the Fab is positioned 29.1 Å away from puromycin, well outside the distance that would be required for the antigen binding site of the Fab to directly contact puromycin via non-covalent interactions.
source: Most strikingly, for this 'best' fit scenario, the Fab is positioned 29.1 Å away from puromycin, well outside the distance that would be required for the antigen binding site of the Fab to directly contact puromycin via non-covalent interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling analysis.

claim: The numerous steric clashes between the Fab and the A site of the ribosome would preclude positioning of the antigen recognition site close enough to recognize puromycin within the PTC of intact ribosomal complexes.
source: Thus, the numerous steric clashes between the Fab and the A site of the ribosome would preclude positioning of the antigen recognition site close enough to recognize puromycin within the PTC of intact ribosomal complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural modeling analysis.

claim: The modeling was conducted using a stalled 80S ribosomal complex in which the ribosomal subunits are in their 'non-rotated' conformational state and the P-site tRNA is in its 'classical' configuration.
source: It is worth noting that our modeling was conducted using a stalled 80S ribosomal complex in which the ribosomal subunits are in their 'non-rotated' conformational state and the P-site tRNA is in its 'classical' configuration (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the structural model used, supported by a citation.

claim: The non-rotated/classical conformation is likely favored in ribosomal complexes stalled by cycloheximide.
source: Although the non-rotated/classical conformation is likely favored in ribosomal complexes stalled by cycloheximide (Budkevich et al., 2011) and emetine (Jiménez et al., 1977), it is conceivable that a minor sub-population of ribosomal complexes becomes chemically fixed in the so-called 'rotated' conformational state in which the tRNAs occupy their 'hybrid' configurations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The non-rotated/classical conformation is likely favored in ribosomal complexes stalled by emetine.
source: Although the non-rotated/classical conformation is likely favored in ribosomal complexes stalled by cycloheximide (Budkevich et al., 2011) and emetine (Jiménez et al., 1977), it is conceivable that a minor sub-population of ribosomal complexes becomes chemically fixed in the so-called 'rotated' conformational state in which the tRNAs occupy their 'hybrid' configurations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the 'rotated' conformational state, the relative rotation of the subunits dramatically narrows the aperture of the A site, making it even less likely that the IgG Fab could access the PTC.
source: In this case, the relative rotation of the subunits dramatically narrows the aperture of the A site, making it even less likely that the IgG Fab could access the PTC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structural changes in the rotated state.

claim: Anti-puromycin antibodies are unlikely to access the interior of intact ribosomes during immunostaining.
source: Overall, these results suggest that anti-puromycin antibodies are unlikely to access the interior of intact ribosomes during immunostaining.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural modeling analysis.

claim: The first major problem with the RPM model is the kinetics of puromycylated NPC release.
source: The first major problem with the RPM model is the kinetics of puromycylated NPC release.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings.

claim: The half-life of puromycylated NPC-ribosome complexes is less than 40 s when cells are pretreated with emetine.
source: We found that the half-life of puromycylated NPC-ribosome complexes is less than 40 s when cells are pretreated with emetine, and extended by only ~2 min with cycloheximide (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The half-life of puromycylated NPC-ribosome complexes is extended by only ~2 min with cycloheximide pretreatment.
source: We found that the half-life of puromycylated NPC-ribosome complexes is less than 40 s when cells are pretreated with emetine, and extended by only ~2 min with cycloheximide (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Once the carboxyl-activated NPC is coupled with puromycin, no further translocation or dissociation of the 80S complex is required for puromycylated NPC release.
source: Although the precise mechanisms underlying these kinetic differences are unknown, our results strongly suggest that once the carboxyl-activated NPC is coupled with puromycin, no further translocation or dissociation of the 80S complex is required for puromycylated NPC release (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Puromycin is small enough to simply bypass the P site tRNA and proceed directly from the PTC through the exit tunnel.
source: We suspect that puromycin is small enough to simply bypass the P site tRNA and proceed directly from the PTC through the exit tunnel.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of puromycylated NPC release.

claim: All SunTag puncta were undetectable at ~5 min after puromycin in all conditions.
source: Critically, all SunTag puncta were undetectable at ~5 min after puromycin in all conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental work shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Even with short incubations at lower puromycin concentrations, labeled NPCs would continue to be released during washing and fixation.
source: Even with short incubations at lower puromycin concentrations, labeled NPCs would continue to be released during washing and fixation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed kinetics of NPC release.

claim: Complete cytoplasmic fixation can take longer than 15 min at room temperature when using conventional 4% paraformaldehyde to fix monolayer cultures.
source: Furthermore, complete cytoplasmic fixation can take longer than 15 min at room temperature when using conventional 4% paraformaldehyde to fix monolayer cultures (Huebinger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: It is likely that the vast majority of puromycylated NPCs are not crosslinked to their ribosomal origin during chemical fixation.
source: Thus, it is likely that the vast majority of puromycylated NPCs are not crosslinked to their ribosomal origin during chemical fixation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics of NPC release and the time required for fixation.

claim: The second major problem with the RPM model is that antibodies are unlikely to directly contact and recognize puromycin within the PTC of fixed, intact ribosomes.
source: The second major problem with the RPM model is that antibodies are unlikely to directly contact and recognize puromycin within the PTC of fixed, intact ribosomes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings from structural modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: Even if a small sub-population of puromycin molecules are retained in the PTC after chemical fixation, structural modeling suggests that these puromycin molecules would be inaccessible during immunostaining.
source: Thus, even if a small sub-population of puromycin molecules are retained in the PTC after chemical fixation, our structural modeling suggests that these puromycin molecules would be inaccessible during immunostaining.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling results.

claim: Based on the kinetics of puromycylated NPC dissociation and inaccessibility of intra-ribosomal puromycin to antibody binding, there should be no general expectation that anti-puromycin immunostaining accurately reports on the original ribosomal translation site.
source: Based on the kinetics of puromycylated NPC dissociation (Figure 3) and inaccessibility of intra-ribosomal puromycin to antibody binding (Figure 4), there should be no general expectation that anti-puromycin immunostaining accurately reports on the original ribosomal translation site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and structural modeling.

claim: The results do not preclude the possibility that released puromycylated NPCs are bound by neighboring proteins, organelles, and/or ribonucleoprotein complexes immediately adjacent to their translation site.
source: However, our results do not preclude the possibility that released puromycylated NPCs are bound by neighboring proteins, organelles, and/or ribonucleoprotein complexes immediately adjacent to their translation site.
evidence: This is a statement about what the results do not rule out.

claim: Nascent polypeptide binding complexes would include canonical targeting motifs such as the signal recognition particle, cytoplasmic chaperones, and neuron-specific RNA granules.
source: Such nascent polypeptide binding complexes would include canonical targeting motifs such as the signal recognition particle, cytoplasmic chaperones (e.g. Hansen et al., 1994), and neuron-specific RNA granules (e.g. Graber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Puromycin-resistant SunTag puncta have been observed in dendrites, and these puncta are thought to contain stalled polyribosomes and NPCs.
source: Indeed, puromycin-resistant SunTag puncta have been observed in dendrites, and these puncta are thought to contain stalled polyribosomes and NPCs (Langille et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The labeling of puromycin-resistant complexes by anti-puromycin IF did not require emetine.
source: Given that emetine does not impede puromycylated NPC release (Figure 3), it is not surprising that the labeling of these complexes by anti-puromycin IF did not require emetine (Langille et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and is consistent with the authors' findings.

claim: The persistence of puromycin at puromycin-resistant sites must require context-specific binding of NPCs within ribonucleoprotein complexes.
source: Instead, the persistence of puromycin at these sites must require context-specific binding of NPCs within these ribonucleoprotein complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' findings and previous literature.

claim: Anti-puromycin IF is unlikely to occur within the ribosome.
source: Since anti-puromycin IF is unlikely to occur within the ribosome (Figure 4), it is likely that these nascent polypeptide interactions occur outside of the ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nascent polypeptide interactions with binding complexes likely occur outside of the ribosome.
source: Since anti-puromycin IF is unlikely to occur within the ribosome (Figure 4), it is likely that these nascent polypeptide interactions occur outside of the ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling results.

claim: The results contribute to growing concerns that PLA can produce false positive signals when both antigens are highly abundant and have overlapping subcellular distributions.
source: Given the implausibility of a true 'RPM-PLA' as we had envisioned (Figure 1), the results of our eL22-HA/Puro PLA also contribute to growing concerns that PLA can produce false positive signals when both antigens are highly abundant and have overlapping subcellular distributions (Alsemarz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and is consistent with the authors' findings.

claim: The issue of 'non-specific proximity' may broadly affect puromycin-based PLAs.
source: This issue of 'non-specific proximity' may broadly affect puromycin-based PLAs (e.g. tom Dieck et al., 2015), as was the case in our study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' findings and supported by a citation.

claim: Typical cultured cells are estimated to harbor at least 1 million ribosomes.
source: Ribosomes are the most abundant macromolecular machine in the cell, with typical cultured cells estimated to harbor at least 1 million ribosomes (Wada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A brief treatment with puromycin will produce an immense number of puromycylated NPCs per cell.
source: Accordingly, even a brief treatment with puromycin will produce an immense number of puromycylated NPCs per cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance of ribosomes.

claim: The eL22-HA/Puro PLA could produce ~200 puncta per cell based solely on non-specific proximity.
source: Viewed through this lens, it is not surprising that our eL22-HA/Puro PLA could produce ~200 puncta per cell based solely on non-specific proximity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance of both antigens and the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The eL22-HA/Puro PLA assay is an outlier in that both antigens are extremely abundant and broadly distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
source: However, it should be noted that our assay is an outlier in this regard, as both antigens are extremely abundant and broadly distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a statement about the specific characteristics of the authors' assay.

claim: The use of direct-conjugated primary antibody PLA probes would be expected to reduce the frequency of false positives.
source: The use of direct-conjugated primary antibody PLA probes would be expected to reduce the frequency of false positives.
evidence: This is an inference about how to improve the PLA technique.
